skills.name: Factorise by grouping and as a difference of two squares

note.text:
Factorising is expanding backwards: write an expression as a product.
• Grouping, for four terms: pair them, take a common factor from each pair, then take out the common bracket. ax + ay + bx + by = a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (a + b)(x + y).
• Difference of two squares: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b). For example x² − 49 = (x + 7)(x − 7) and 9x² − 4 = (3x + 2)(3x − 2).
Always take out a common number factor first: 2x² − 18 = 2(x² − 9) = 2(x + 3)(x − 3).
A sum of two squares, such as x² + 9, does not factorise this way.
Check any factorisation by expanding it again.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to factorise four-term expressions by grouping and any difference of two squares, taking out common factors first.
Builds on: Lesson {2} (expansion and the product (a + b)(a − b)); Form Three common factors.
Leads to: factorising quadratic trinomials and solving quadratic equations by factorisation.

sections.heading: Grouping four terms
sections.text:
Some expressions have four terms and no factor common to all of them, such as xy + {mono(3, 'x')} + {mono(5, 'y')} + {15}.
• Pair the terms: (xy + {mono(3, 'x')}) + ({mono(5, 'y')} + {15}).
• Take a factor out of each pair: x(y + {3}) + {5}(y + {3}).
• Both parts now share the bracket (y + {3}). Take it out: (x + {5})(y + {3}).
If the brackets do not match, try pairing the terms differently. Expand your answer to check it.

sections.heading: The difference of two squares

key_words.meaning: write an expression as a product of factors
a number or letter that divides every term
pairing terms so that each pair has a common factor and the pairs share a bracket
go on until no factor can be split further

mistake.why: ({poly([1, 'x'], [-5, ''])})² expands to {quad(1, -10, 25)}. A difference of two squares needs one plus and one minus bracket.

steps: Group the terms in pairs: (xy + {mono(p, 'x')}) + ({mono(q, 'y')} + {p * q}).
Take x out of the first pair and {q} out of the second: x({poly([1, 'y'], [p, ''])}) + {q}({poly([1, 'y'], [p, ''])}).
The bracket ({poly([1, 'y'], [p, ''])}) is common to both: take it out.

cards.idea: Grouping: pair the four terms, take a common factor out of each pair, then take out the bracket they share.
A difference of two squares factorises as (first + second)(first − second), where first and second are the square roots.
Look for a common number factor first. What is left is often a difference of two squares.

misconceptions.explain: 'Completely' means keep going: x² − {a * a} still factorises as {lin2(1, a, 1, -a)}.
Expand it: {lin2(k, a, 1, -a)} has a middle term. Take {k} out in front instead.
{k}({poly([1, 'x'], [-a, ''])})² = {k}({quad(1, -2 * a, a * a)}): that has a middle term.

solution: Take out the common factor {k}: {k}({quad(1, 0, -a * a)}).
x² − {a * a} is a difference of two squares: {lin2(1, a, 1, -a)}.

misconceptions.explain: ({poly([1, 'x'], [-a, ''])})² = {quad(1, -2 * a, a * a)}: it has a middle term and a plus sign at the end.
Use the square root of {a * a}, which is {a}: {lin2(1, a, 1, -a)}.
{a * a} has no x, so x is not a common factor.
That is only part way: {q}(x + {p}) also has the bracket (x + {p}), so take it out of both.
Taking {q} out of {mono(q, 'x')} + {p * q} leaves x + {p}, not x + {p * q}.
Take the square root of the whole term {mono(a * a, 'x²')}: it is {mono(a, 'x')}, in both brackets.
Use {b}, the square root of {b * b}, in both brackets.
{lin2(a, b, a, b)} = ({poly([a, 'x'], [b, ''])})², which ends with +{b * b}. One bracket needs a minus sign.

solution: a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b) with a = {mono(a, 'x')} and b = {b}.

misconceptions.explain: 'Completely' means keep going: x² − {a * a} still factorises as {lin2(1, a, 1, -a)}.
Expand it: {lin2(k, a, 1, -a)} has a middle term. Take {k} out in front instead.
{k}({poly([1, 'x'], [-a, ''])})² = {k}({quad(1, -2 * a, a * a)}): that has a middle term.

solution: Take out the common factor {k}: {k}({quad(1, 0, -a * a)}).
x² − {a * a} is a difference of two squares: {lin2(1, a, 1, -a)}.

questions.prompt: Use a difference of two squares to calculate {n}² − {m}² without squaring the large numbers.

misconceptions.explain: a² − b² is not (a − b)². Use ({n} + {m})({n} − {m}).
{n}² − {m}² is not {n} − {m}. Multiply the sum by the difference: {n + m} × {n - m}.
